what_it_measures: Research volume in robotics. Read as a growth rate against the same quarter a year earlier, never as a level — the level reflects how large the field already is, and only the rate carries information about acceleration.
caveat: arXiv category membership is author-declared and cs.RO absorbs a large amount of work that is really machine learning with a robot in the title. The category grows partly because tagging habits change.

what_it_measures: New repositories created in the window. Builder adoption sits closer to commercialisation than research volume, so a divergence between this and the arXiv line — papers rising while repositories flatten — is the more interesting reading.
caveat: Topic labels are voluntary and fashion-driven. A rise can reflect relabelling rather than new work, and GitHub's search index excludes repositories that were later deleted or made private. Year-over-year is deliberately not computed for this source: GitHub prunes deleted and dormant repositories from its search index, so a past window returns only survivors and a naive comparison overstates growth several-fold. The level is recorded; the comparison becomes available from this store's own history after a year.

what_it_measures: Downloads of the dominant open robot-learning library. Package downloads are the noisiest signal in the ladder but the fastest to move.
caveat: Download counts include continuous integration runs and mirrors, which can exceed human use by an order of magnitude. Treat step changes with suspicion — they are usually a new CI pipeline, not new users.

what_it_measures: Instrumentation and methods research, chosen over the general astrophysics categories because it tracks building things rather than observing them.
caveat: This category is dominated by ground-based telescope instrumentation, which has little to do with orbital economics. It is a weak proxy and is included provisionally.

what_it_measures: New spacecraft-related repositories. Low absolute volume, so it functions as a presence check rather than a trend line.
caveat: Volume is low enough that quarter-to-quarter movement is mostly noise. Do not read a single quarter; require four. what_it_measures: Downloads of the main orbital mechanics library, as a proxy for the number of people computing satellite positions for any purpose.
caveat: Widely used in amateur astronomy and satellite tracking hobby projects, so the majority of this number has no commercial content at all.

what_it_measures: Biomolecules research volume.
caveat: Thin. This category runs at roughly two hundred submissions a quarter, which is low enough that Poisson noise dominates any trend shorter than several years. Biology also preprints predominantly to bioRxiv rather than arXiv, so this measures a small and possibly unrepresentative slice.

what_it_measures: New synthetic biology repositories, as a check on whether the field has developer-facing tooling at all.
caveat: Expected to be very low. A persistently near-zero reading is itself the finding — a substrate with no developer ecosystem is not behaving like the internet or AI did at the equivalent stage. Year-over-year is deliberately not computed for this source: GitHub prunes deleted and dormant repositories from its search index, so a past window returns only survivors and a naive comparison overstates growth several-fold. The level is recorded; the comparison becomes available from this store's own history after a year.

what_it_measures: Downloads of the long-established computational biology library, as a floor measure of bioinformatics activity.
caveat: Mature and near-universal in the field, so it tracks the size of the existing discipline rather than any acceleration. Useful as a denominator, not as a signal.

what_it_measures: Quantum research volume. This candidate fails the substrate test, so the specific thing being watched is whether publication growth is accompanied by any movement in the builder-adoption rows below it.
caveat: A large and well-funded academic field will produce steady publication growth regardless of commercial prospects. Rising submissions here are close to uninformative on their own, which is precisely why they are paired.

what_it_measures: New quantum computing repositories.
caveat: Heavily weighted towards tutorials, coursework and simulator experiments rather than production work. Volume here has historically been decoupled from commercial deployment. what_it_measures: Downloads of the dominant quantum SDK.
caveat: Almost all of this runs against simulators rather than hardware, so it measures interest in learning quantum programming, not demand for quantum computation.

what_it_measures: Neurons and cognition research volume.
caveat: Thin, and dominated by computational neuroscience that has no interface component. A weak proxy retained until a better one is identified.

caveat: Tracks academic neuroscience broadly. Its relationship to interface commercialisation is indirect at best.

caveat: Software activity is a poor proxy for a theme whose constraints are chemical and industrial. Included for completeness rather than conviction. what_it_measures: Downloads of the battery modelling framework, as a proxy for the number of people simulating cell behaviour.
caveat: Small and research-dominated. Movement will be driven by academic term dates as much as by anything commercial.

what_it_measures: Machine learning research volume, tracked not as a candidate but as a calibration line. Every candidate above should be read against this: it is what a confirmed exponential looks like in the same units, on the same axis.
caveat: Now so large that it is decelerating in percentage terms simply through base effects. A mature exponential flattens on a ratio chart long before it stops mattering, which is a caution against reading a falling growth rate as a failing theme.

what_it_measures: Downloads of the dominant JavaScript AI SDK, as the builder-adoption calibration line.
caveat: A single vendor's package standing in for an ecosystem. It reflects that vendor's competitive position as much as the field's growth.

what_it_measures: Downloads of the most widely installed LLM application framework, as the Python-side calibration line.
caveat: Framework fashion moves faster than the underlying field, so a decline here may mean developers moved to a competitor rather than away from the theme.

what_it_measures: Cumulative stars and last-push date on the original artifact. Included as the fringe calibration line: this is what the reference case looks like today, seventeen years after it was dismissed on a mailing list.
caveat: A cumulative count only ever rises, so the level is meaningless and only the rate of change carries information. The last-push date is the more useful field — it answers whether the artifact is still alive, which is the question that mattered in 2010.

what_it_measures: The second calibration line, showing the slow version of the pattern.
caveat: Specification repositories accumulate stars from people bookmarking a reference document rather than building on it, so this overstates activity relative to a code repository.

what_it_measures: Activity on one of the leading FHE implementations. Watch the push date at least as closely as the star count.
caveat: A single vendor s library. Its decline could mean the field is fading or that developers moved to a competing implementation, and the star count alone cannot distinguish those.

what_it_measures: A second FHE implementation, tracked alongside the first so that a divergence between them can be distinguished from a decline in the field.
caveat: Corporate-backed research libraries can remain nominally maintained long after internal interest has ended. Commit frequency is a better liveness test than the existence of recent commits.

what_it_measures: Cryptography and security research volume, as the upstream line for the FHE entry.
caveat: Far broader than FHE, so it will barely move on FHE-specific developments. It functions as a denominator: FHE mattering would show as this category growing unusually, not as this category growing.
